questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the camera took over from painting
questions.learningObjective: identify the role photography displaced when it became available
questions.stem: Before photography, a painted portrait was the ordinary way to record what a person looked like. Once photographic portraits could be made in numbers, which role of painting was most directly taken over?

options.text: The recording of appearances, since light and a lens could fix a likeness without a trained hand
The making of images of the gods, since a camera cannot photograph anything that is not present
options.misconception: believes a camera records only what physically exists, forgetting posed and arranged sittings

options.text: The training of painters, since a sitter would no longer sit for an artist at all
options.misconception: thinks sittings stopped once photography arrived, when they continued for decades

options.text: The decoration of churches, since a photograph was far too cheap to be used on a large commission
options.misconception: assumes photographs were used in churches, where painted altarpieces remained the normal medium

questions.explanation: The displaced role is the record of likeness, and the reason is practical rather than artistic. A camera needs no training to operate, costs little per sitting, and produces a fixed image that can be duplicated, so a person could be recorded without sitting through a slow and expensive painted sitting. That left painting with the things the camera could not do: invention, composition, colour, the imagined, the impossible. The two are not rivals, since most painters kept using photography as a source, but the division of labour between recording and imagining is what the invention set in place.
questions.hint: Ask which of painting's jobs could be done by a machine and a chemist, and which could not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What indexicality does and does not license
questions.learningObjective: state what a photograph's causal link to its subject can be used to argue
questions.stem: A photograph is called indexical because light from the scene actually fell on the light-sensitive surface. What does that causal link let the photograph be used to prove, and what does it not let it prove?

options.text: It licenses the claim that something was in front of the lens; it does not license the claim that the picture is the whole truth
It licenses the claim that the image is an exact copy, since no hand touches the film during an exposure
options.misconception: believes a causal link makes an exact copy, ignoring framing, timing and every other decision

options.text: It licenses the claim that the photograph is unbiased, since the chemistry is identical in every exposure
options.misconception: thinks the chemistry neutralises the photographer's choices, confusing the process with the picture

options.text: It licenses the claim that the image is unique, since each negative fixes one scene for ever
options.misconception: confuses uniqueness with indexicality, which are independent properties of an image

questions.explanation: Indexical means there is a physical chain from the scene to the record: light from a thing in front of the lens reached a particular patch of emulsion and made a mark. That is a real warrant for one narrow claim, that what is pictured was there at that moment during that exposure. It warrants nothing about the picture's completeness, about whether the situation was arranged, about whether the moment is typical, or about whether anything was added afterwards in the darkroom. The term is therefore routinely over-read: an indexical image is evidence, and evidence has to be interpreted, corroborated and tested.
questions.hint: Ask what the chain of light from subject to emulsion actually proves, and what it leaves open.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The limits of indexicality as testimony
questions.learningObjective: weigh an indexical claim against the photographer's decisions
questions.stem: A photograph shows a crowd at a factory gate; the photographer arranged the workers, waited for the light, and cropped the owner's house out of the frame. What does the indexical relation establish in that case?

options.text: That those people were at that gate at that hour, and nothing at all about the conditions being photographed
That the factory was a decent place to work, since the arrangement shows how contented the workers were
options.misconception: reads a posed arrangement as testimony to the workers' conditions

options.text: That the scene is unposed, since a causal link between light and film cannot be arranged in advance
options.misconception: believes the causal link guarantees an unposed scene, forgetting the photographer's staging

options.text: That the crowd is typical, since one photograph is a fair sample of everything that happened there
options.misconception: treats a single frame as a representative sample of an unobserved day

questions.explanation: The exposure establishes presence and nothing else. The workers were at the gate, at that hour, and the light that made the mark came from them, which is a genuine documentary fact and the strongest thing the picture can be used for. Everything the photograph is being asked to prove about conditions depends on the photographer's decisions: he chose the hour, the angle, the people, and what to leave outside the frame. Reading the crop as a description of the whole situation is the standard error, and it is why the crop itself has to be examined as evidence.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the picture is a trace of what was there, and which part is a decision about what to include.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What mechanical reproduction does to originality
questions.learningObjective: explain how mechanical reproduction alters the status of an image
questions.stem: A photographic image can be printed many times, and each print is nearly identical to every other. What does that do to the idea of the unique, hand-made original?

options.text: It detaches the image from any single hand-made object, so copies can circulate while the image itself is repeatable
It destroys the value of the image, since a picture is only worth what there is one of
options.misconception: believes value comes only from scarcity, ignoring that a widely reproduced image can be powerful

options.text: It proves the print inferior to the negative, since the negative is the only unique object in the process
options.misconception: confuses the negative's uniqueness with the image's, so the image is treated as the lesser object

options.text: It makes every print a separate work, since each impression is made at a different moment by a different hand
options.misconception: believes each impression is a distinct artwork, which would dissolve the meaning of reproduction

questions.explanation: Reproduction separates an image from any one object that carries it. The same picture can now be in a book, on a wall, in a newspaper and in a classroom, and none of those is the original, because there is no original in that sense: there is a negative, a printing process, and an image that recurs. That is the condition most modern art has to work in, and it makes questions of edition, provenance and the status of the support matter in a new way. It also changes the audience's relation to a picture, from one encounter in one room to many.
questions.hint: Ask what is actually unique in a reproducible process, and whether that is the image or its carrier.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a manifesto is for
questions.learningObjective: state the function a manifesto performs for a group
questions.stem: Artists who had not been working to a shared programme publish a short text setting out a common aim and inventing a name for it, and the text is then read as the moment the group became coherent. What is a manifesto for?

options.text: Declaring aims in advance and supplying a name, so scattered works can be recognised as one project afterwards
Recording finished works, so that later scholars can learn exactly what the group went on to do
options.misconception: confuses a programme stated in advance with a record compiled afterwards

options.text: Setting out prices and commissions, so that the group can arrange its own sales without dealers
options.misconception: believes a manifesto is a business document, confusing a declaration of aims with administration

options.text: Replacing the works themselves, since a written programme is the more durable contribution to art
options.misconception: thinks a text can substitute for works, inverting the relation between statement and practice

questions.explanation: A manifesto is prospective. It declares what the writers intend, invents or adopts a term that can be applied to what they make, and recruits by giving others a reason to join. That work is only possible in advance, and its effect is retrospective: once a criterion exists, later work can be recognised, judged and even excluded by it. The weakness follows from the same feature. A group can adopt a programme without producing the works, and artists can outgrow a text written in their name, which is one reason manifestos are read as records of intention rather than of achievement.
questions.hint: Ask whether the text is written before or after the works, and what it gives the group that the works could not.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Refusing the gallery system
questions.learningObjective: identify what an alternative exhibition channel was intended to change
questions.stem: Artists who refused to show through the established dealers set up co-operative galleries, small alternative rooms and their own printing presses. What were they trying to change?

options.text: Who decides what is shown and who is shown, by replacing a dealer-controlled channel with one they control
How paintings are made, since an alternative room supplies a different technique of painting
options.misconception: believes a new venue changes the medium, confusing an institution with a technique

options.text: How much art costs, since a co-operative may set any price it likes without a dealer involved
options.misconception: thinks the point was price control, which the dealer system had already settled in advance

options.text: Who pays for art, since a self-run gallery can be financed entirely by the artists who hang it
options.misconception: assumes self-organising removes the money problem, ignoring rent, insurance and publicity

questions.explanation: The institution was the target, not the medium or the price. A dealer-run channel decided which artists were shown, in what company, and to whom, and an artist outside it had no way in except by being bought. Co-operatives, independent societies, alternative spaces and small presses shifted that control: membership decided the programme, exhibitions were more frequent and cheaper to fail, and the audience was a chosen public rather than whoever passed the commercial gallery. The limits were equally real, since a co-operative develops its own hierarchies and the market still sets the price.
questions.hint: Ask who the gatekeeper was in the system being refused, and who takes that role in the alternative.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A critique made from inside the market
questions.learningObjective: explain why using the market's own data is a strong form of critique
questions.stem: In one exhibition, sheets were printed that carried, laid out like banknotes, the actual prices at which the other artists in the show had recently sold. What is that work doing?

options.text: Using the trade's own records to make the trade its subject, so the accusation is measured in its own units
Selling those artists' work at a loss, so the exhibition is an act of charity rather than a critique
options.misconception: reads the display as charity, confusing a printed price with a transfer of funds

options.text: Reproducing the artists' signatures, so the sheets pass as currency and deceive the buyers
options.misconception: believes the sheets imitate currency in order to deceive, confusing appropriation with fraud

options.text: Paying each artist a share of the takings, so the exhibition redistributes money rather than displaying it
options.misconception: assumes printing prices distributes money, when it only puts figures on a wall

questions.explanation: The tactic's strength is that it is checkable. The figures come from the trade, not from the artist's rhetoric, so the accusation is specific and falsifiable, and the audience is the market's own audience, which means the people named cannot dismiss it as polemic. There is also an uncomfortable implication, since the work's force depends on the market it attacks, so the piece cannot claim to stand outside the system. A pure denunciation, by contrast, restates a position without producing any evidence, and can be answered with a counter-praise without anyone having to produce a single number.
questions.hint: Ask where the numbers came from, and who is in a position to check them.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Abstraction as a decision about subject
questions.learningObjective: characterise abstraction as a decision rather than a technique
questions.stem: Across a series, an artist removes every recognisable object until only bands, grids and flat colour remain. What has the artist decided, and what has the decision cost?

options.text: That the subject is no longer what makes a painting matter, so composition alone has to carry the whole work
That the artist has run out of ability, since the figure is the hardest thing in art to paint well
options.misconception: reads abstraction as a failure of technique rather than a decision about subject matter

options.text: That the paintings are unfinished, and that the missing subject will be supplied later by the viewer
options.misconception: believes a removed subject is still supplied invisibly, so the painting stays representational

options.text: That colour alone records light exactly, so the subject is only a redundant piece of physics
options.misconception: thinks abstraction is scientific accuracy, confusing optical description with art

questions.explanation: Removing the subject is a decision about what a painting is for. If nothing is recognisable, the picture cannot narrate, persuade or depict, and everything that holds it has to come from relations: the interval between shapes, the edge where one field meets another, the weight of one colour against another. The cost is equally plain. The viewer loses the entry that a subject provides and has to construct the field themselves, which is why such work was read at first as empty and why the initial reception was often hostile. The trade is deliberate: legibility is given up so that relation can be looked at.
questions.hint: Ask what has to do the work of holding the picture together once the subject has gone.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What colour field scale does to looking
questions.learningObjective: explain the perceptual effect of a colour field's scale
questions.stem: Large fields of a single colour are hung so that the picture is about as tall as the viewer and extends beyond the edge of vision. What does that scale do to the act of looking?

options.text: It puts the colour in the viewer's field of vision rather than in front of it, so the work becomes an environment
It shows the skill needed to lay a large flat area evenly, which is the difficult part of the technique
options.misconception: believes scale is about technical difficulty, when the effect on perception is the point

options.text: It makes the colour easier to reproduce, since a flat field has no brushwork for a print to record
options.misconception: thinks the scale serves reproduction, which is a concern of printing rather than of the work

options.text: It reduces the number of colours the viewer must compare, so the effect becomes simpler to read
options.misconception: believes fewer colours is easier to read, ignoring what a field does to the body of the viewer

questions.explanation: Scale changes the viewer's physical relation to the picture. A field taller than the viewer and wider than the field of vision cannot be taken in at once, so the edge is never seen and the work stops behaving like a picture of something. What the viewer experiences instead is a change in their own field of vision as they move, which is why walking up to a colour field alters it and why the edge is the most active part of the surface. The colour becomes an event in the viewer's perception rather than a description of a thing outside.
questions.hint: Ask where the viewer's eye can be at any moment, and whether the picture's edge is ever visible.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What makes a performance a work
questions.learningObjective: identify the conditions that constitute a performance
questions.stem: A work consists of a body moving through a room for a stated duration before an audience, and afterwards only photographs and a set of instructions remain. What makes that a work rather than something that merely happened?

options.text: The conditions are constitutive: body, duration, site and audience are specified, and they are what any repetition follows
The photographs, since a work only begins to exist once it has been fixed in a reproducible form
options.misconception: believes documentation is constitutive, confusing a surviving trace with the work itself

options.text: The artist's intention, since the plan is the work and the evening is only its execution
options.misconception: equates a plan with the work, the claim conceptual art later put to the test

options.text: The audience's recollection, since the work lives on in the memory of those who were present
options.misconception: locates the work in memory, ignoring that the conditions were specified in advance

questions.explanation: A performance is a work when its conditions are specified: what is done, by and with whose body, for how long, in which place, before which kind of audience. Those conditions are repeatable in the sense that a score or a set of instructions can be followed, and it is the specification, not the one-off evening, that is the work's content. Documentation is therefore a trace and an incomplete one, usually a few flat frames of something that happened in time. The distinction is what makes performance hard to collect, hard to reproduce and easy to misdescribe as an event.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be written down for the work to be performed again, and whether that document is the work.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that is a set of instructions
questions.learningObjective: explain how instructions can constitute a work
questions.stem: A typed sheet hangs in a gallery: a numbered list of instructions for an action that nobody has performed, with no object and no image on the wall. What is the work?

options.text: The instructions, which specify what would be done and are complete without ever being executed
The execution, for which the sheet is only a script and which has not yet taken place
options.misconception: believes a score is only a script, missing that the specification can be the finished work

options.text: The intention of the writer, which no reader can verify and which therefore cannot be the work
options.misconception: tries to make a work depend on a state of mind, which nobody else can check

options.text: The paper and the typing, so that the material support of the statement is the artistic content
options.misconception: reduces the work to its support, confusing the object on the wall with the statement it carries

questions.explanation: The move is to treat the proposition as the work. A list of instructions is a complete artistic object because it specifies the work fully: any reader can say what it proposes, and the proposal is what the artist has made, whether or not anyone carries it out. That is what dematerialisation means, and it is why the work can be reduced to a sheet of paper and a frame while becoming harder to collect, insure, exhibit and sell. The convention is also what makes the work arguable, since the question of whether instructions can be art is raised by the object rather than by a claim about art.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statement needs anything else to be complete, and who decides what it asks for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an installation depends on its site
questions.learningObjective: explain what an installation loses when separated from its room
questions.stem: A work fills a room with objects, sound and dim light, and it makes no sense photographed: without the room, the parts are a heap of things. What does that dependence tell you about the work?

options.text: The site is part of what the work says, so moving it changes the work and may end it entirely
The work is really the objects, and the room is only the container the lender happened to supply
options.misconception: believes the container is incidental, when the container is constitutive of the work

options.text: The work is its documentation, and the room is a rehearsal space for the photographs
options.misconception: reduces the work to its reproduction, which is precisely what the piece refuses

options.text: The work is the viewer's walk through the room, so what is actually installed does not matter
options.misconception: makes the viewer the only content, ignoring what has been installed and arranged

questions.explanation: The room is constitutive, not incidental. It fixes the sequence in which things are met, the scale of each object relative to a body, the level of light, the acoustic conditions and the direction of travel, and every one of those is part of the meaning. Installed elsewhere, the same inventory of objects produces a different work, and often an incoherent one. This is what makes such work difficult to lend, to store and to show twice, and it is why its documentation is always a translation that has to be recognised as a loss rather than read as a substitute.
questions.hint: Ask what the room decides about the objects, and whether that could be reproduced anywhere else.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The readymade and the question of authorship
questions.learningObjective: state the question a ready-made raises about authorship
questions.stem: An artist buys a factory-made object, signs it, and exhibits it unaltered, arguing that the act of selection is the art. What question does the work put on the table?

options.text: Whether authorship belongs to the one who makes the thing or to the one who chooses what will be seen and called art
Whether the object was badly made, since only good workmanship would justify showing it at all
options.misconception: judges a ready-made by its workmanship, applying a craft test the work rejects

options.text: Whether a museum should buy it, given that only a unique handmade object can be collected
options.misconception: believes collectability settles the question, confusing the market with authorship

options.text: Whether the artist's signature is enough to make the object original rather than a copy of something else
options.misconception: thinks a signature makes an object original, which is a claim about law rather than about art

questions.explanation: The ready-made relocates the artistic act. If a mass-produced object can be made into art by being chosen, signed, placed and named, then the making is not what confers the status, and the criteria people actually use to recognise art have to be examined: context, intention, the frame, the signature, the institution. That is why the work was so provocative and why it generates arguments about the artist's role, about the market's role in conferring value, and about whether the museum's collecting was ever about more than paperwork. The craftsmanship objection misses the point, since the objection is precisely not about craftsmanship.
questions.hint: Ask what has changed if the object was made in a factory, and which of the usual tests of art value survives that.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What collage does to drawing and making
questions.learningObjective: explain how collage blurs the line between drawing and making
questions.stem: An artist glues cut printed fragments into a picture: newsprint, a strip of wallpaper, part of a map, with charcoal lines drawn across them. What has the technique done to the idea of drawing and making?

options.text: It has joined the two: the work is drawn and composed, yet assembled from found matter rather than applied by hand
It has abolished drawing, since nothing in the work was drawn by the artist's own hand at all
options.misconception: believes nothing is drawn, ignoring the planning and the drawn elements of the composition

options.text: It has made the work a copy, since every fragment comes from an image that was already printed
options.misconception: thinks found material makes a work derivative, which is the accusation usually levelled at collage

options.text: It has turned the work into a sculpture, since the pasted layers give the surface real depth
options.misconception: infers sculpture from layering, confusing a low relief with a constructed object

questions.explanation: Collage is the technique in which drawing and making become the same activity. The composition is planned and often drawn, but it is realised by cutting and pasting objects that already carry images, so the finished work is partly a drawing and partly an assembly of things not made here. That is what allowed cheap printed matter, and the fragments of many viewpoints at once, into serious painting, and it is why the technique was resisted as borrowing and is now read as a challenge to the idea of originality itself. The pieces sit on the surface, but that flatness is the point of the device, not a sculpture.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the picture is drawn and how much is found, and what the flatness of the surface is for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Photomontage as political argument
questions.learningObjective: explain what photomontage makes possible that a single photograph does not
questions.stem: Photographs of separate people and places are cut and rearranged so that one head sits on another body in an incongruous setting, and the result appears in a political magazine as a comment on a speech. What does the technique make possible?

options.text: An argument built out of evidence, since real photographed elements are combined to assert what was never photographed
A more accurate likeness, since the cut edges remove the distortion of the original camera lens
options.misconception: believes cutting improves accuracy, confusing the lens with the montage

options.text: A cheaper image, since reassembling fragments costs far less than commissioning a new photograph
options.misconception: reduces the technique to an economy, ignoring the claim being constructed

options.text: A private joke, since the incongruity is a matter of humour between the reader and the maker
options.misconception: reads a published political claim as a private joke between maker and reader

questions.explanation: Photomontage borrows the authority of documentary and spends it on an assertion. Each element is a genuine photograph, so the parts look evidenced, but the relation between them has been invented, and the invention is the point. That is what makes the device useful for polemic: it can put a person in a place they were not and let the picture make the accusation, in a form that reads as documented rather than drawn. It is also why the method is ethically double-edged, since the same authority that carries a critique can carry a lie, and readers have to be able to detect the joins.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the picture are traces of real events, and where the claim actually comes from.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Mural and its public audience
questions.learningObjective: infer what a public audience forces on a wall painting
questions.stem: A painter covers the walls of a public building with figures that must be legible from across a square, and the commission specifies a broad public rather than a private viewer. What does that audience force?

options.text: Legibility at distance and a scale that addresses a crowd, so the detail cannot be made for a near viewer
A much smaller scale, since a broad public must be able to take in every figure at once in detail
options.misconception: believes a public audience needs small scale, reversing what legibility at distance requires

options.text: A private key, since a subject shown in public requires an explanation only the owner can read
options.misconception: invents an esoteric reading, when the whole purpose is public address

options.text: One fixed viewpoint, since a crowd can only stand in a single place in front of the image
options.misconception: assumes a crowd stands still and frontal, ignoring that public images are seen in motion

questions.explanation: The audience fixes the conditions of viewing, and those conditions fix the design. A wall painting read from a distance needs large, clearly separated figures, few of them, and a composition that survives being seen briefly and obliquely; the minute finish of a private panel is wasted on it. The square itself becomes the room the work was made for, and its walls become a sequence experienced while walking, not a single frontal vista. That is also where the politics sit, because painting a public building's interior for a general public is also a claim about who belongs in the nation's story.
questions.hint: Ask how far away the work will first be seen from, and what that distance does to the level of detail.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A memorial and its site
questions.learningObjective: interpret the choice of site as part of a memorial's meaning
questions.stem: A memorial is cut into the ground as a long descending path between two dark walls carrying names, rather than raised on a pedestal in an open square. What is the site being made to do?

options.text: To place the visitor physically inside the event, so the descent and the wall of names are part of the meaning
To keep the cost down, since carving into earth takes far less material than casting a figure
options.misconception: assumes the choice is economic, when it is formal and experiential

options.text: To keep the subject out of public view, so that the dead are not discussed in a busy square
options.misconception: believes a ground-level cut is hidden, when it is highly public and highly visible

options.text: To leave room for more, since a cut in the ground can be extended whenever more names are needed
options.misconception: thinks the site can simply grow, missing that the work was completed as a design

questions.explanation: In a memorial the site is part of the argument, and here the site is doing most of the work. Descending between two walls puts the visitor below ground level, which reads as entering the event rather than observing it, and the list of names makes the scale of loss a matter of counting rather than of representation. Nothing had to be said on a pedestal, because the ground, the descent and the wall carry the claim. That is also why such sites attract argument: the choice of place is an assertion about whose loss is national, and it can be contested on the same grounds as any other representation.
questions.hint: Ask what the visitor's body does at this memorial, and how that differs from standing before a statue.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Whom a monument commemorates
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the political content of keeping or removing a monument
questions.stem: A city debates whether to keep, move or remove a statue of a figure whose career included conquest, and which faces a community that reads its presence as a claim about them. What makes the argument political rather than merely aesthetic?

options.text: Whom the figure is taken to stand for, and what his presence in that place asserts, both of which are historical judgements
The quality of the bronze, since a badly cast statue cannot be defended on any grounds at all
options.misconception: reduces a claim about meaning to a technical one, which is the usual way of avoiding it

options.text: The cost of moving it, since the public will accept any decision that is cheap enough
options.misconception: believes money settles a question of historical meaning

options.text: The age of the statue, since anything a century old is automatically beyond criticism
options.misconception: assumes age confers immunity from judgement, which is the opposite of a critical position

questions.explanation: A monument is a public claim about who counts, made in a durable public medium, and that is what makes it contestable. The same object can be read as honour and as domination depending on who stands in front of it, and no property of the bronze settles that, because the argument is about the figure's relation to the community that now lives there. Keeping, moving, contextualising and removing are all available contemporary responses, and each is a statement about whose history is national. The aesthetic and financial questions are real but they are the form the question takes, not the substance of it.
questions.hint: Ask who the figure is said to represent, and what his presence in that square asserts to the people who live there.

questions.topic: How an archive photograph frames its subject
questions.learningObjective: analyse how framing shapes the claim made by an archive photograph
questions.stem: A photograph taken as part of a survey of working life shows a group of children, sharply lit and plainly posed, and the photographer noted that he wanted the conditions to be evident. How does the framing shape that claim?

options.text: It chooses which activity and which faces are in view, so the picture argues through what it includes and omits
It does not shape the claim at all, since a photograph records the whole scene and framing is only technical
options.misconception: believes the frame is neutral, confusing the field of view with the field of attention

options.text: It shows the children were healthy, since a sharp and well-lit image is evidence of good conditions
options.misconception: reads technical quality as evidence of welfare, a common and consequential error

options.text: It shows the children were working, since a posed group in a photograph must have been at work
options.misconception: assumes posing implies a single activity, which a posed group portrait denies

questions.explanation: Framing is an argument, and the survey photograph is not an exception. The photographer chose where to stand, how close, what to include, when to expose and what to leave outside the edge, and each of those choices shapes what the picture can be said to show. The pose in particular is doing something that a candid shot would not: it makes the children available to the camera's requirements, which is a fact about the photograph and not about their lives. The claim that conditions are evident therefore has to be tested against the evidence of how the picture was made, not accepted from its subject matter.
questions.hint: Ask which of the photographer's decisions would still be visible in the print if the scene were described in words.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a documentary claim is a claim
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a documentary claim from a verified fact
questions.stem: A photographer spends years recording one district and presents the pictures as evidence of how the people there live. What makes the truth claim a claim rather than a fact?

options.text: The pictures are selections, arranged and timed, that a viewer cannot check, so the claim rests on trust as well as on the record
The pictures are all true, so the claim is a matter of fact and not of interpretation at all
options.misconception: treats a photographic record as self-authenticating, the assumption being tested

options.text: The project appears in a book, so the truth lies in the text and the pictures merely illustrate it
options.misconception: believes the caption carries the truth, subordinating the image to the text

options.text: The project was funded by a sponsor, so the photographs are compromised and carry no claim whatever
options.misconception: assumes a sponsor invalidates the record, which is a different kind of criticism

questions.explanation: A documentary claim is an assertion about a world assembled out of selections. Which moment was chosen, which people, which angle, and above all which of the many things that happened were photographed at all: none of that is visible in the print, and all of it determines what the print appears to be evidence of. The word documentary imports the authority of a legal or administrative record, and that authority is exactly what has to be earned. The critical questions are therefore about process and provenance, and a photographer who staged a scene has weakened the claim without necessarily making the picture worthless.
questions.hint: Ask what a viewer cannot see in the print, and how much of the claim depends on those invisible decisions.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the video form adds
questions.learningObjective: explain what duration and succession contribute to a video work
questions.stem: A work is projected as a sequence of images over forty minutes and is shown as video rather than hung as a set of prints. What does the video form add to the still image?

options.text: Duration and succession, so meaning can be carried by order, pace and what follows what
Colour accuracy, since video reproduces colour better than a photographic print can do
options.misconception: believes video's advantage is colour fidelity, a technical rather than a formal gain

options.text: Authenticity, since a moving image cannot be staged the way a single photograph can
options.misconception: thinks a moving image cannot be staged, which is not the case at all

options.text: Reproducibility, since a video can be copied and shown again without any loss of quality
options.misconception: credits video with reproducibility, which it shares with prints and paintings

questions.explanation: The difference is the addition of time as a material. A print presents a whole field at once and its parts are simultaneous; a video presents a succession in which the order of shots, their length and their pace produce the meaning, and a cut can make an argument that no single frame makes. Sound enters as another layer, and the work becomes something that happens rather than something that is present. That also weakens any claim to be simply documentary, since the material is selected and assembled by editing, and it introduces a new fragility, because a video has to be played on equipment that will one day fail.
questions.hint: Ask what a print cannot do with two images that a video can, and what a cut is doing.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What the ear notices
questions.learningObjective: describe what a sound work offers that a visual one does not
questions.stem: A work consists only of recorded sound, and the room the speakers stand in changes what the listener hears. What does the ear supply that the eye does not?

options.text: Duration, direction and texture through time, so the material is a sequence located in space
Colour, since a listener perceives a sound work's tone in the same way a painter perceives hue
options.misconception: transfers a visual category to the ear, which is the classic cross-sensory error

options.text: Scale, since the ear is the only sense able to judge the size of a building directly
options.misconception: believes the ear judges size directly, when it judges direction and distance at best

options.text: Line, since a sound has a contour that can be drawn and compared like a drawn line
options.misconception: treats a sonic contour as a drawn line, which erases the dimension of time

questions.explanation: Sound's medium is time, and it is heard as it unfolds rather than all at once, so succession and duration are structural rather than decorative. The ear is also unusually sensitive to direction and to texture, which is how a listener locates a source and hears a surface, and it detects layering and rhythm without being able to see them. The room is part of the work, since reverberation and reflections alter the sound, so the same recording in a different space is a different work. A recording captures the signal and loses the room, which is the difficulty sound work has with documentation.
questions.hint: Ask how long the eye takes in a painting compared with a sound, and what the room does to what is heard.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a participatory work assigns to the viewer
questions.learningObjective: state the role a participatory work gives its participants
questions.stem: In one work the composition is not given: it is produced by what the participants do, and no result is preferred over any other. What has the work assigned to the viewer?

options.text: The work of making the decisions, so authorship is shared between the artist who sets terms and those who act
The work of buying a ticket, since participation in the arts has always meant supporting them
options.misconception: equates participation with patronage, which is a payment rather than an act

options.text: The work of learning a technique, since the artist has a finished result in mind for people to reach
options.misconception: believes there is a hidden correct result, which denies that the work is open

options.text: The work of applauding, since a responsive audience completes a performance that is otherwise fixed
options.misconception: treats a responsive audience as a participating one

questions.explanation: Participation moves the artistic work from the object to the process, and the decisions that used to be the artist's become the participants'. The artist still sets the terms, which is where the authorship now sits: the conditions, the materials, what will be counted as an instance. The consequences for institutions are practical rather than theoretical, since there is no object to acquire, so what gets collected and catalogued is documentation, and the room has to be given over to people rather than looked at. An audience that applauds is responsive, not participatory, and the distinction is the whole content of such a work.
questions.hint: Ask who decides what the result will be, and where the artist's contribution now sits.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A work that a label excludes
questions.learningObjective: test a movement's stated criterion against a work shown with it
questions.stem: A show presents itself as a survey of a movement defined by pure abstraction, and among the works is one made by gluing printed fragments and a found object into a relief. What does that inclusion do to the claim?

options.text: It puts before the audience a work the stated criterion excludes, so the claim must be narrowed or given up
It strengthens the show, since an exception of this kind demonstrates the movement's range and vitality
options.misconception: treats a contradiction as support, inverting the logic of a definition

options.text: It proves the movement's aim was misreported, so the inclusion is evidence against the show's own catalogue
options.misconception: jumps from a weak definition to a claim about the catalogue's honesty

options.text: It proves the work is not by the artist it is attributed to, so the label is beside the point
options.misconception: assumes an out-of-style work must be misattributed rather than the category wrong

questions.explanation: A label that defines a movement by a criterion is making a claim that can be tested, and a work that fails the test is evidence about the claim. That is the discipline that keeps descriptions honest: movements are known by what their practitioners made, so the honest response to an exception is to widen the definition, to treat the work as a late development, or to explain why the exception belongs. The other readings each dodge the evidence, and one of them, that a misattribution explains the difficulty, is a possibility that has to be argued rather than assumed in either direction.
questions.hint: Ask whether the work meets the stated test, and what a definition has to do when a work fails it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Repetition and the interval
questions.learningObjective: explain what repetition and interval do in a serial work
questions.stem: An artist fills a room with identical factory-made units set at regular intervals, so the eye reads one unit, then the gap, then the unit again. What is the repetition doing there?

options.text: Making the interval and the module the subject, so attention moves to the logic of the system itself
Making the units more valuable, since many copies of a good object must be worth more than one
options.misconception: believes quantity raises value, a market error read as a formal one

options.text: Hiding the individual object, since the artist has said the units are interchangeable in fact as well as form
options.misconception: overreads the metaphor, claiming an interchangeability the objects deny

options.text: Saving the cost of making original work, which is the practical reason for all the repetition
options.misconception: reduces a formal decision to an economy

questions.explanation: When a unit does not change, the only variable left is the arrangement, so the arrangement becomes what the work is about. The viewer's attention shifts from any one object to the relation between objects: the interval, the grid, the edge, the way the room's dimensions divide up. Using factory production is part of the method rather than a saving, because it removes the trace of the hand and leaves the system legible, and it invites comparison with the readymade, where the same object is simply bought. The risk of the method is that the system can collapse into a list, which is why the interval has to be made to matter.
questions.hint: Ask what changes from one unit to the next, and what the viewer is being asked to notice instead.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The rhetoric of the propaganda poster
questions.learningObjective: identify the viewing conditions a propaganda poster is designed for
questions.stem: A state poster reduces its message to a few flat colours, a single figure seen from below, and one short imperative line of type. What is the visual rhetoric doing?

options.text: Making one idea instantly legible to a crowd in motion, using size, angle and contrast before the words are read
Presenting the complexity of the message, since many small elements let a passing reader study the details
options.misconception: believes a poster rewards close reading, when it is built for people in motion

options.text: Persuading by evidence, since a depicted figure is more reliable testimony than a statement in words
options.misconception: treats a painted figure as testimony, confusing image with witness

options.text: Persuading by beauty, since a well-composed image convinces where argument would fail
options.misconception: assumes beauty persuades on its own, ignoring the poster's imperative function

questions.explanation: The poster's design is fixed by its viewing conditions: large, on a wall, seen for a second or two by someone walking or driving past, and often seen many times a day. That forces reduction to a few elements, a limited palette that can be printed cheaply and read at distance, and typography that survives a glance. Seeing a figure from below makes it dominant, and an imperative verb converts a description into an instruction, which is the point: the poster is not describing a world, it is telling a reader to act. The reduction is what makes it work and also what makes it so easy to reproduce endlessly.
questions.hint: Ask how long a passer-by has, and what design decisions that limit forces on the poster.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The countercultural poster
questions.learningObjective: explain what a countercultural poster does with its style
questions.stem: A countercultural poster announces a benefit concert, its hand-drawn lettering warping and overlapping a photographic figure, and its main slogan demands that a law be changed. What distinguishes it from official publicity?

options.text: It speaks to a constituency defined by a position, so the collision and distortion carry the politics
It is made from cheaper materials, since hand lettering costs less than machine-set type
options.misconception: reduces a style to a production economy, confusing means with meaning

options.text: It avoids identifiable people, since portraits of individuals were officially prohibited at the time
options.misconception: invents an image ban, when the real risk was prosecution of the publisher

options.text: It is printed outside the country, since domestic printers would not handle dissenting material
options.misconception: infers a printing location from a hand-drawn style, which proves nothing about it

questions.explanation: The style is the affiliation. Hand-drawn lettering that breaks the rules of commercial typography, overprinted photographs, and dense imagery read as outside the professional system of advertising, which is exactly the identification the poster is selling to its audience. The slogan then gives that style a position rather than a product to sell, and the imperative gives the viewer something to do. The method was cheap to produce and easy to distribute on city surfaces, so it built a shared visual language among people who had no access to the official one, which is why the style outlived the campaigns that used it.
questions.hint: Ask who the poster is speaking to, and what a rule-breaking style tells the reader about the maker.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The feminist critique of the pose
questions.learningObjective: identify the strategy of a critique that works on representation itself
questions.stem: An artist takes the standard pose used to teach drawing and re-stages it so that the viewer's own position in the picture is exposed. What is the strategy?

options.text: Showing that the arrangement of bodies in a picture is a choice about who looks and who is looked at
Proving the pose is anatomically impossible, since an inverted figure cannot be drawn at all
options.misconception: believes the critique rests on anatomical error, confusing argument with drawing

options.text: Banning the pose for good, so that no figure from that academic tradition may be shown again
options.misconception: confuses criticism of a convention with a prohibition on a subject

options.text: Training the viewer to draw better, since the critique is really a lesson in proportion
options.misconception: reads a political intervention as a technical exercise

questions.explanation: The pose is a technology of looking, and re-staging it makes the mechanism visible instead of invisible. By working inside the tradition the work inherits, quoting its own authority, the critique is harder to dismiss as ignorance of the craft, and what becomes arguable is the arrangement itself: which body is active, which is available to be looked at, and where the viewer has been placed. The same line of work treats the domestic and the everyday as political subject matter and rearranges the canon itself, since a list of great artists can be answered by a list of names that the list excluded.
questions.hint: Ask what the pose does to the relationship between the figures and the person looking at it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Chance and the found object
questions.learningObjective: state what chance operations change about the making of a work
questions.stem: A group of artists combines found objects so that the final combination was not fully decided in advance, and insists that the result is not a failure of control. What is the method for?

options.text: Letting the meeting of unrelated things propose the work, so the artistic act becomes selection and framing
Producing a finished object faster, since improvisation removes the need to design anything in advance
options.misconception: believes chance is a shortcut, confusing method with speed

options.text: Rejecting skill altogether, since any handmade object would serve the purpose of this one equally well
options.misconception: equates all handmade objects, missing the selection that carries the meaning

options.text: Reproducing chance exactly, since a random outcome can be recorded and then repeated identically
options.misconception: believes chance can be repeated, which is the one thing chance never is

questions.explanation: Working by chance or by found material relocates the artistic act from invention to recognition. The artist does not stop making decisions, but the decisions change kind: what to gather, when to stop, and how to frame and present what the meeting of things produced. That was a deliberate rejection of the idea that a work's value lies in the originality of its maker, and of the bourgeois taste that made the found object valuable. It also carries a real risk, since without the framing decision the result is just a heap, which is exactly the failure the group is arguing against.
questions.hint: Ask where the decisions still are, if the combination was not planned in advance.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a wall text does to a pair of works
questions.learningObjective: interpret the interpretive work done by a label
questions.stem: Two works are hung side by side, and the wall text calls one a study for a portrait and the other a finished painting, though their surfaces and sizes are otherwise similar. What has the label changed?

options.text: It proposes a relation and a status, so a visitor reads the pair as preparation and result
It dates both works, since a study must always be earlier than the painting it prepares
options.misconception: believes a study is always earlier, which is a chronological claim the label does not settle

options.text: It identifies the materials, since a wall text is a technical description of the support and ground
options.misconception: reduces a label to a technical caption, ignoring its interpretive work

options.text: It removes the need to look, since the label tells the visitor what to see in both pictures
options.misconception: thinks the label replaces looking, when in fact it directs it

questions.explanation: A label is an argument, and this one argues for a hierarchy by proposing a relationship between two things that look similar. Once the terms study and finished are supplied, the visitor reads one work as incomplete and the other as resolved, and a decision has been made about intention that the objects themselves do not make. That is why labels are contested and why they can be shown to be wrong: a material examination may find that both works are equally finished, which would make the label an interpretation rather than a fact. It does not stop the looking; it organises it.
questions.hint: Ask what the two words in the label let the visitor assume that the surfaces do not show.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An exposure that recorded duration
questions.learningObjective: read what an exposure records in a described photograph
questions.stem: A photograph shows a woman at a table: the light comes from a window on her left, her moving hands are recorded as blurred streaks, and the table edge and the wall behind her are sharp. What has that exposure recorded?

options.text: Light arriving over an interval, long enough for the movement to record while the still things stay sharp
The sitter's intended gesture, since a slow exposure is what lets a person hold a position steady
options.misconception: believes a long exposure makes a gesture steady, when it makes movement visible

options.text: A single indivisible moment, since a photographic exposure cannot last long enough to blur anything
options.misconception: thinks an exposure is instantaneous, ignoring the length of the shutter interval

options.text: The photographer's memory of the room, since a camera fixes what the eye has already assembled
options.misconception: treats a photograph as a memory, which inverts the causal order of the process

questions.explanation: An exposure is an interval during which light reaches the emulsion, and everything printed is an average of that interval. A short exposure gives an instant and freezes motion; a longer one records duration, and a hand that moved is averaged into a smear while the table, which did not move, stays sharp. The sharp background is a choice of focus and aperture rather than a fact about the room. What the print therefore bears witness to is a light event of a particular length made under particular conditions, which is exactly why it can be evidence of a person's presence and not of what that person meant.
questions.hint: Ask how long the film was open for, and what an average over that interval does to a moving hand.

questions.topic: A collage described from its parts
questions.learningObjective: analyse a described collage for its combination of found and made material
questions.stem: A picture is built by pasting printed fragments, a mechanical diagram, a strip of wallpaper and a painted eye, with charcoal lines drawn straight across all of them. What has the artist done that matters?

options.text: Combined found and made material, so the work is drawn and assembled at once and the fragments keep their origins
Copied a single source image, since every fragment comes from a picture that was made by somebody else
options.misconception: treats found material as copying, which is the charge usually levelled at the technique

options.text: Completed the surface in one session, since the charcoal lines show the picture being finished on the spot
options.misconception: reads a drawn line as proof the work was finished in a single session

options.text: Removed the difference between drawing and collage, so that only one of the two can honestly be said to occur
options.misconception: believes a combination erases the categories, where it actually crosses them

questions.explanation: The fragments keep their own origins: the diagram carries the logic of an instruction, the wallpaper a pattern and a domestic surface, the eye a piece of a painting. What the artist adds is a single drawn structure that ties kinds of image that normally never meet into one space, so the picture is simultaneously found and made, flat and layered, borrowed and composed. That is why the technique was attacked as theft and why it is now read as a claim about how images are built in the first place, including out of printed information rather than out of nature.
questions.hint: Ask what the drawn lines are doing across the fragments, and whether the parts have lost their own character.

questions.topic: A photomontage in a political magazine
questions.learningObjective: infer the argument a photomontage makes
questions.stem: A magazine picture shows a suited figure whose head has been replaced with another man's, and behind him an unrelated landscape has been inserted, with hard cut edges visible at the joins. What is the picture arguing?

options.text: That the two men are connected, using the look of evidence for a relationship no exposure recorded
That the photograph is a composite, since visible cut edges are the surest sign of a fabricated image
options.misconception: believes the cut edges are there to confess, when they are the price of the illusion

options.text: That the landscape stands for the man's patriotism, since landscape always signifies a nation
options.misconception: reads landscape as a fixed national symbol, which the insertion itself puts in doubt

options.text: That the figure has been caricatured, since changing a head turns any photograph into satire
options.misconception: assumes a changed head means caricature, which is only one of several readings

The hard edges are what print does to any cut-out, not a confession, since the intention is that the joins be read without being noticed. The device is therefore an argument in the form of testimony: it puts a man in a place he was not and lets the image make the charge, which is far more effective than a drawn accusation and far harder to answer. questions.hint: Ask which parts are traces of real events, and where the connection between them actually comes from.

questions.learningObjective: interpret the labelling of an unaltered found object as part of a work

Whether the object is well made, since a factory product is being shown to be judged as a crafted object

options.text: Whether the label is accurate, since a false manufacturer would make the whole work a forgery
options.misconception: treats the accuracy of the label as the artistic question, confusing a record with a claim

questions.topic: Colour fields in a bare room
questions.learningObjective: infer the perceptual effect of scale in a described installation
questions.stem: Two large fields of colour hang on adjacent walls of a bare room, each taller than the viewer, so that turning and stepping back is needed to see either one whole. What is the viewer experiencing?

options.text: A change in their own field of vision as they move, since the edges never enter the view at once
A skill in laying large flat areas evenly, which is the difficulty the scale exists to display
options.misconception: reads scale as a display of manual skill, missing what the work does to the viewer's body

options.text: A comparison between two colours, which adjacent walls set up for a direct side-by-side judgement
options.misconception: believes adjacent fields exist for comparison, when the geometry of the room is the point

options.text: A sense of the room's size, since a large picture always enlarges the space it hangs in
options.misconception: assumes a large picture enlarges a room, which is a claim about decoration

questions.explanation: The point of the scale is that the work cannot be taken in. A field taller than the viewer and wider than the field of vision has no visible edge from inside the room, so the viewer is not looking at a picture of something but standing inside a change in their own vision, which shifts as they turn. That is why the edge is the most active part of such a surface: it is the only place where the picture ends. The bare room exists to make that body-scale relationship unavoidable, and the effect disappears in a reproduction, which is why these works are shown as objects rather than as images.
questions.hint: Ask whether the viewer can ever see the whole work at once, and what their body has to do for it to register.

The blurred photographs, since a work begins to exist only once it has been fixed in reproducible form
options.misconception: makes the trace constitutive, confusing documentation with the work itself

options.text: The loft, since the building is what survives while the evening itself is entirely lost
options.misconception: treats the venue as the work, confusing a container with a set of conditions

That gap is the practical difficulty of the form, and it is why a museum ends up acquiring the documentation and calling it the work. The building was a condition rather than the content, and the audience attended rather than constituted it.

questions.explanation: The list is the work, because it specifies the work completely and the specification is what the artist has made. Nothing is missing because nothing was pending: the sentences describe actions and the work asserts those descriptions as its content, which is also why they are phrased as negations, since a refusal to act is as describable as an act. The frame and the wall text then become carriers rather than components. The consequence is a set of practical difficulties, since such a work is difficult to insure, exhibit, collect and sell, and it forces the question of whether an instruction can be art onto the object itself.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: An installation that depends on its room
questions.learningObjective: identify what a described installation's site contributes
questions.stem: A visitor walks through a room in which the ceiling lowers steadily towards the far end, the light enters through one high opening on the near wall, and objects lie along a path on the floor. What does the room contribute?

options.text: A sequence and a body-scale, since the falling ceiling and the single light govern how the visitor moves and sees
Shelter and nothing more, since the same objects would mean the same thing in any room of the same size
options.misconception: believes the room is incidental, missing the sequence and the light that it controls

options.text: A neutral container, so that the arrangement of the objects along the path is the whole of the work
options.misconception: treats the container as neutral, when it is doing most of the work

options.text: A setting for photography, since the room was designed to be photographed from a single viewpoint
options.misconception: assumes a designed room exists to be photographed, reversing cause and record

A ceiling that descends towards the far end is a gradient the visitor's body registers before the eye explains it, so the space tells the visitor how to move and what to expect; the single high opening sets the direction of the light and leaves most of the floor in shadow. The objects along the path are read differently at every step because the space changes around them. Relocate the inventory and you have a different work, often a failed one, and a photograph, which flattens the sequence into one view, cannot record any of it.
questions.hint: Ask what the falling ceiling does to the visitor's body, and what the single opening leaves dark.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A memorial cut into the ground
questions.learningObjective: interpret what a described memorial asks of its visitors
questions.stem: A long dark wall is set into the ground in a V, with names cut into it in tight rows, and visitors walk down between the arms to the point where the two walls meet. What does the design ask of the visitor?

options.text: A descent into the ground, so the act of walking down becomes part of what the memorial states
A close reading, since the small carved names can be read only by someone standing near the wall
options.misconception: reads the small lettering as a device for privacy rather than for closeness

options.text: A complete circuit, since two arms set in a V are meant to be followed all the way round and back
options.misconception: assumes a V can be walked as a full circuit, which its geometry denies

options.text: Silence, since the design is intended to keep visitors quiet enough for the names to be heard
options.misconception: assigns a sound instruction to a design that says nothing about noise

questions.explanation: The design asks for a bodily act. Walking down between the walls puts the visitor below the level of the surrounding ground, which reads as entering the event rather than standing outside it, and the two arms converge so the descent ends at a focus. The names are cut in rows because the point is the count: a list makes the loss measurable and specific, which a figure or a word could not do. Nothing is said in the imperative, yet the whole site is a claim about whose loss belongs to the nation, and that claim is why such sites are argued over rather than merely visited.
questions.hint: Ask what the visitor's body is doing that a visitor to a statue does not do.

questions.topic: A poster read from a distance
questions.learningObjective: identify the viewing condition a described poster is designed for
questions.stem: A poster fills a wall with one flat colour, a single figure with a raised arm, and three words in capitals at the bottom that read as a command. Which viewing condition does that design serve?

options.text: A crowd moving past, since one colour, one figure and three words can be taken in at a glance and at distance
Close study, since the large empty field of colour leaves room for a viewer to add detail of their own
options.misconception: believes empty space invites elaboration, when the emptiness is what makes the reduction work

options.text: Private reading, since capitals are chosen to be legible only at arm's length on the wall
options.misconception: confuses capitals with near viewing, when capitals serve distance

options.text: Repeated display, since a single figure can be reprinted at many sizes without losing any of its force
options.misconception: confuses a property of the design with print economy, which is not the reason for it

questions.explanation: Every decision follows from where and for how long the poster is seen. A wall, a few seconds, a viewer in motion, and often the same wall seen repeatedly over weeks, all of which push towards reduction: one colour that prints cheaply and reads at distance, one figure large enough to be identified instantly, and a line of capitals that can be taken in at a glance. The imperative mood is the part that does the persuading, since it converts a description into an instruction, and the figure seen from below supplies the hierarchy. The design is legible by design, which is also why it can be reproduced without loss.
questions.hint: Ask how long a passer-by has, and what that rules out as well as what it demands.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A shooting log with a second exposure
questions.learningObjective: interpret a processing record as evidence about the whole of a photograph
questions.stem: An exhibition record lists one photograph: a single exposure, printed 30 cm on 30 cm paper from a negative, with a note that the sky was added by a longer exposure on the same negative from a second negative made months later. What does the record establish?

options.text: That light from the scene reached the film, and that the printed sky came from a different occasion entirely
That the whole image is unaltered, since both exposures were made with the same camera and lens
options.misconception: believes a second exposure is still a single record, ignoring what was added to the negative

options.text: That the picture is a copy of an earlier photograph, since two exposures cannot make one document
options.misconception: thinks combining two negatives makes the result a copy, which is not what the process produces

options.text: That the print is unique, since a composite negative is only ever made once and cannot be repeated
options.misconception: confuses the uniqueness of a negative with the uniqueness of the image it makes

questions.explanation: Every exposure on a negative is an indexical trace of light that came from something in front of the camera at that moment, so the ground, the figures and the light on them have a date and a place. The sky is different in kind: it was recorded on another negative, at another time, and transferred, so the finished print asserts a relationship between two occasions that never existed together. That makes the record unusually valuable to a historian, since it fixes the moment of the subject while exposing the moment of the sky as constructed, and it means the picture can no longer be used as evidence of a single moment's weather.
questions.hint: Ask which parts of the print are traces of one event, and which part is a transfer from another.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A print run and a facsimile edition
questions.learningObjective: interpret a circulation record as evidence about originality
questions.stem: A museum record lists a photograph exhibited once, twelve prints made of which five were sold, and a publisher who has since issued thousands of facsimiles. What does the record do to the idea of a unique original?

options.text: It relocates uniqueness to the negative and the exposure, since the image itself is now serial and circulating
It shows the image is a copy, since a work that exists in thousands can no longer be the work itself
options.misconception: reduces a reproducible image to a copy, confusing the carrier with the work

options.text: It shows the work is a multiple, so the impressions should be catalogued one number at a time
options.misconception: counts impressions as the work, which turns a serial image into a set of objects

options.text: It shows the twelve prints are the work, since they are the only objects any viewer will see
options.misconception: privileges the small edition, when the facsimiles are what actually reached the public

questions.explanation: The record makes the ordinary condition of photographic images explicit: the picture is repeatable, and the thing that is not repeatable is the exposure and its negative. Twelve prints and thousands of facsimiles are not degradations of an original but the forms in which the image exists, and the fact that the facsimiles vastly outnumber the prints tells you something the prints alone would not, namely that the image's public life is in the book and the wall, not in the gallery. The consequence for value is the reason originality had to be redefined somewhere else in the argument.
questions.hint: Ask which object in the process is unique, and where the work is said to be located.

questions.topic: Sixty units counted in an installation
questions.learningObjective: interpret a counted serial arrangement as evidence of a method
questions.stem: An installation record lists sixty identical factory-made units arranged in six rows of ten, every interval exactly 30 cm, with no unit altered, replaced or reoriented. What does the count establish about the work?

options.text: That the module and the interval are the content, since the units are deliberately identical and unvaried
That the work is about abundance, since a larger number of units must produce a larger effect
options.misconception: believes quantity is the measure of effect, confusing the size of a set with its system

options.text: That the units are valuable, since sixty examples of one form must be worth more than a single example
options.misconception: reads multiplicity as value, a market confusion presented as a formal one

options.text: That the work is handmade, since no factory could produce sixty identical objects and set them out true
options.misconception: supposes identical units imply hand labour, reversing the point the record makes

questions.hint: Ask what the viewer's eye can distinguish between one unit and the next, and what is left to look at.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A survey of how a photograph was framed
questions.learningObjective: read a framing record as evidence of the photographer's decisions
questions.stem: A survey of a photograph records that the frame cuts the crowd at the waist, sets the horizon on the lower third, and includes a factory chimney just inside the right edge. What does that record show about the framing?

options.text: That the crop and the inclusions are decisions, so the picture argues through what it includes and omits
That the photograph caught the whole scene, since whatever is in the record was necessarily in the original view
options.misconception: believes a record of a crop is a record of the scene, confusing the field of view with the field of attention

options.text: That the crowd was at work, since a horizon set on the lower third always records labour in progress
options.misconception: reads a compositional device as evidence of activity, a habitual symbolic guess

options.text: That the chimney was an accident, since a survey records only what happened to be behind the lens
options.misconception: treats a documented placement as chance, when the survey is a record of choices

questions.explanation: A framing record is a record of decisions, and each entry here is one. Cutting the crowd at the waist is a compositional choice that makes figures read as a mass rather than as individuals. Putting the horizon on the lower third is another compositional choice, and it tilts the picture towards the ground the crowd occupies. The chimney is the clearest case, because an object just inside the edge is normally kept out; including it shows the photographer knew it was there and judged that the picture needed it, which is an argument about industry being part of the scene. Nothing here can be explained by luck, and nothing here is evidence of what the crowd was doing.
questions.hint: Ask which of these three facts a camera would produce on its own, without a person deciding.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A participation record with no fixed result
questions.learningObjective: interpret a record of a participatory work
questions.stem: A work is documented as requiring a stated number of participants in each session, and the artist's notes say the arrangement is produced by what the participants do and was never fixed in advance. What is the work made of?

options.text: The stated conditions and the decisions taken in each session, so there is no single object to acquire
The list of components used, since a full inventory is what makes a work repeatable anywhere
options.misconception: believes an inventory is sufficient, which is the assumption of an object-based account

options.text: The number of participants, since attendance is the only measurable part of such a work
options.misconception: reduces the work to attendance, which is bookkeeping rather than description

options.text: The artist's plan, since the written conditions are the work and the sessions only perform them
options.misconception: makes the plan the whole work, which the artist's own notes contradict

questions.explanation: The record separates the two halves of the authorship. The stated number of participants and the conditions are the artist's contribution, and they are the part that can be repeated. The arrangement produced in a session is the participants' contribution, and it is not recoverable afterwards, because it existed only while the session ran and was never fixed. So the record describes a process and its rules, and there is no object behind them for a collection to acquire. That is the practical reason institutions end up cataloguing documentation, and the reason the documentation is always a description of a rule rather than a copy of a thing.
questions.hint: Ask which part of this would still exist after everyone had gone home.
