questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A video log tested against a claim of truth
questions.learningObjective: test a claim of unmediated record against an editing record
questions.stem: A work is catalogued as forty-five minutes long with three hundred and twelve cuts, and the accompanying statement says that nothing in it is staged. What does the record do to that claim?

options.text: It shows a cut roughly every nine seconds, so the material is selected and assembled whatever the claim says
It confirms the claim, since a running time of forty-five minutes cannot be faked in a studio
options.misconception: believes length proves actuality, which is the assumption a cut rate undermines

options.text: It shows the work is a record, since only documentary material is ever cut at that rate
options.misconception: equates rapid cutting with documentary truth, confusing method with subject matter

options.text: It shows the claim is beside the point, since the running time alone decides what the work contains
options.misconception: decides the content by duration alone, ignoring what the cuts are doing

questions.explanation: The arithmetic is the argument: three hundred and twelve cuts in forty-five minutes is a cut every nine seconds or so, and a cutting rate of that order is the signature of selection and juxtaposition rather than of continuous observation. Whether individual moments were staged is a separate question, and a careful account would have to allow that some were and some were not. What the edit establishes regardless is that the material was assembled, so the statement that nothing is staged cannot be used to claim that the work is unmediated. A documentary claim has to survive its own construction being made visible.
questions.hint: Divide the number of cuts by the running time, and ask what that rate tells you about how the material was chosen.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Where uniqueness goes when an image repeats
questions.learningObjective: state the effect of reproduction and where uniqueness is relocated
questions.stem: A photographic image is printed in five hundred identical impressions and a publisher circulates them widely. First say what that does to the idea of the image as a unique object, and then say where the uniqueness in the process now sits.

options.text: It detaches the image from any single object, and the uniqueness shifts to the negative and the exposure
It makes the image more valuable, since a rare process and a common subject are both involved in it
options.misconception: believes reproduction raises value, importing scarcity as the only measure of worth

options.text: It removes all value, since a work of art must exist only once in order to be a work of art
options.misconception: assumes uniqueness is the definition of art, which no account of a print requires

options.text: It makes the image a mere copy, so the negative becomes the work and everything printed is secondary
options.misconception: reduces the image to a copy, confusing the medium of display with the work itself

questions.explanation: Reproduction separates an image from any object that carries it, so the image can be in a book, on a wall and on a screen at once, and none of those is the original, because there is no original in that sense. What remains unique is the act of exposing the negative and the negative itself, and calling either of those the work is a category decision that has to be argued rather than assumed. The social consequences follow from the same fact: many viewers, repeated encounters, an image that can be detached from any single setting, and therefore a value that has to rest on something other than rarity.
questions.hint: Ask which object in the process exists once, and whether that object is the image or its support.

questions.learningObjective: evaluate what an alternative exhibition channel changed and what it did not
questions.stem: Artists in one city formed a co-operative gallery with no dealer, showing members' work and selling directly to the public. First say what the arrangement changed, and then say what it could not change.

options.text: It changed who decides what is shown and who sells, but it could not make itself free of internal hierarchy
It changed the medium of the works, since a co-operative supplies its own materials to its members
options.misconception: believes a new institution changes how the work is made

options.text: It changed the price of everything sold, since selling directly removes the market in a single step
options.misconception: assumes removing the dealer removes the market, which still sets prices and records sales

options.text: It changed the audience, since a co-operative has no public and shows only to its own members
options.misconception: believes a co-operative has no public, when reaching one is the whole point of it

questions.explanation: What changed was control of the channel. Membership rather than a dealer decided the programme, exhibitions could be frequent and cheap to fail, and the audience was a public the group had chosen rather than whoever passed a commercial gallery. What did not change is equally instructive: the market continued to set the prices and to record the sales that made a career possible, the group had to compete for the same attention, and a membership is not democracy, since reputation and seniority reproduce hierarchies inside it. The refusal was real and the institution it created had its own costs.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the programme, and then ask who still decided what the work was worth.

questions.learningObjective: weigh a trace of an event against an image that has been composed
questions.stem: A log records one exposure, and the print shows a figure with one hand added in over a longer exposure on the same negative. First say what the light on the negative proves, and then say what the second exposure does to the claim.

options.text: It proves light from the scene reached the negative, and the added hand makes the picture composed
It proves the whole scene is documented, and the second exposure only corrects a sky that was too bright
options.misconception: believes a documented scene is a whole scene, ignoring selection and addition

options.text: It proves nothing at all, since a negative carrying two exposures is by definition not a photograph
options.misconception: dismisses any worked negative, which would also rule out ordinary exposure control

options.text: It proves the figure was standing there, and the second exposure merely deepens a light background
options.misconception: confuses an addition with a tonal adjustment, since only one of them adds something

questions.explanation: An exposure is a causal trace: light from something in front of the lens reached a patch of the negative, which is a real warrant for the presence of a figure and for the light around it. The second exposure adds a hand that was never in the same moment as the body beside it, so the finished print asserts a relationship no single occasion contained. The result is a construction assembled out of traces, which is the ordinary condition of a worked negative, and the practical consequence is a division in what the picture can be used to prove: strong for the body and the setting, weak for the whole of the event as it happened.
questions.hint: Ask what one exposure can witness, and then ask what the second one adds that the first never saw.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish the record of an installation from the experience of it
questions.stem: A catalogue records an installation as a list of objects, a plan and a set of measurements, and notes that it has been shown only once. First say what that record gives a reader, and then say what it cannot give.

options.text: It gives the components, their arrangement and their dimensions, but not the walk, the light or the felt scale
It gives everything a visitor experienced, since a complete record of the parts is a complete record
options.misconception: believes a parts list is a complete record, confusing a specification with an experience

options.text: It gives only the title, since the arrangement and the measurements are the artist's private business
options.misconception: dismisses the measurements, which are the one precisely recordable part of it

options.text: It gives the sequence and the scale, and it cannot show which of the components the artist made
options.misconception: answers a question about authorship rather than about what a visitor can receive

Everything that constituted the experience is missing from it by nature rather than by negligence, because the work's content was the sequence of encounters, the time spent in the room, the level of light at that hour, the acoustics, and the way the space registered on a moving body. A photograph flatters itself into looking like a substitute by being a single view at a single instant, which is the opposite of what the work was. The record is therefore a translation, and the honest thing is to state what it drops.
questions.hint: Ask what a plan can record, and then ask where a visitor was standing when the work happened.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order of work in a photomontage
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of making a photomontage for publication
questions.stem: A photomontage is being made for a magazine that will print it at page size. Put these four stages into the order in which they must be performed.

Choose the source photographs whose parts are going to carry the argument
Cut the selected photographs to the shapes that the composition requires
Add drawn or typed elements that state what the montage is arguing

questions.explanation: The order is forced by what each stage needs from the one before it. Selection comes first, because you can only cut what you have chosen, and because which photographs are available decides what the argument can be made out of at all. Cutting follows selection, since the shapes are determined by the composition you intend, and it has to be done before anything is laid down. The drawn or typed element is added once the picture is settled, because it names the claim and a claim stated before the evidence is in place will not match it. Reproduction is last, and it is the stage that makes the joins visible, which is why the montage is a print form rather than a unique object.
questions.hint: Ask what each stage requires to exist first, and which stage is only possible once the argument is settled.

questions.topic: The order of work in a woodcut print
questions.learningObjective: sequence the stages of pulling a relief print

Cut away the areas that are not to print, leaving the image standing up in relief

Register the sheet on the block, with the inked face of the block against the paper

The sheet is registered on the inked relief and burnished so that the pressure transfers the film of ink, and only then does an impression exist. Signing and numbering come last of all, because the edition is counted as the prints are pulled, and a number is a record of an act, not a plan.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What indexicality is worth as evidence
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the evidentiary value of a causal link between image and subject
questions.stem: Explain what a photograph's causal connection to its subject does and does not make it good as evidence, and say how far a reader may rely on it.

answer.exemplar: Begin with the chain, because the chain is what the word indexical names. Light leaves a thing in front of the lens, travels through the lens, and reaches a particular patch of light-sensitive material, where it changes that patch and no other. Each mark on the negative is therefore a causal consequence of something having been in front of the camera during that exposure, and that is a stronger warrant than any hand-made image can offer, because there is no step in the chain at which an intention inserts itself. From that warrant a narrow inference follows: something was there, at that moment, in that light. Note what does not follow. The chain says nothing about whether that something was the point of the picture, whether the moment was typical or exceptional, whether the people were told where to stand, whether the camera was level, how much was outside the frame, whether anything was removed later in the darkroom, or whether the caption describing it is true. Those are all facts about the making, and the making is as much an artefact as the subject. A strong answer then draws the practical consequence. Because the image is a witness rather than a record of the whole, it has to be interrogated like one: the process has to be established, the crop examined, the prints compared, the caption checked against what the picture shows, and the account corroborated by other evidence. The commonest failure is the substitution of indexicality for truth, the assumption that a causal link to the world guarantees that the picture tells the whole story about it. The second commonest is to swing the other way and dismiss every photograph as mere interpretation, which throws away a real and useful warrant. The defensible position is in between: a photograph is unusually good evidence that something was in front of the lens, and no evidence at all on its own about what that something meant.

questions.explanation: A full answer names the physical chain, states the one inference it licenses, lists several it does not, and ends with what a reader or curator must therefore do about provenance, process and corroboration. A weak response either equates indexicality with truth, or dismisses photography as pure interpretation without saying what the causal link is worth.
questions.hint: Ask what the light actually did, and then ask how many conclusions that single fact supports.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a manifesto does and what it costs
questions.learningObjective: evaluate a manifesto as an instrument as well as a statement
questions.stem: Explain what a manifesto does for a group of artists, and what it costs them. Do not treat it as only a statement of intention.

answer.exemplar: A manifesto is an instrument, and the first thing to say is what it is an instrument for. It declares aims in advance, which fixes the group against charges of having no programme. It supplies vocabulary, often by inventing or adopting a single term, and that word is the most portable thing the group produces: a stranger can be told what the work is by being given the word. It recruits, because the word is an invitation, and it creates criteria, which is the part with the longest consequences. Once a criterion exists, work can be judged against it, including work that is hostile to it, and later observers will use the same criterion when they decide what belongs. It also creates a public and, usually, a scandal, and the scandal is functional, since being noticed is one of the few ways to change who is looking. Now the costs. A manifesto is written at one moment, so it dates the work and can be overtaken by it: an artist who outgrows the programme is read as a heretic or as a trajectory, and the text becomes an obstacle. It makes the work legible only as an illustration of the theory, which forecloses readings the text did not anticipate and hands the critics the vocabulary of the manifesto rather than of the work. It invites parody and pastiche, since a declared aim is a set of instructions that anyone can follow. And it appears to settle the question of whether this is art in advance, by assertion, which is a claim about the world that the works then have to carry on their own. A weak answer treats the manifesto as pure intention and stops there, or condemns it as rhetoric without noticing that it changed the terms on which the work was received.

questions.explanation: A full answer gives the prospective functions, naming, recruitment and criteria, and then the costs of fixing a programme, dating the work, and answering the is-it-art question by assertion. A weak response summarises what the text says instead of what the text does.
questions.hint: Ask what the text does to a stranger who has never seen the work, and then what it costs the writers.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a site cannot be replaced by a photograph
questions.learningObjective: explain the limits of documentation for a site-dependent work
questions.stem: Explain why an installation that depends on its site cannot be understood from a photograph of it, and say what its documentation has to give up.

answer.exemplar: The reason is that the work's content is not the inventory of objects but the experience of moving through a particular space, and a photograph cannot hold any of the properties that make an experience spatial in time. It gives one viewpoint, at one moment, from one height, and it therefore fixes what is in fact variable. A visitor to an installation is not stationary: the ceiling may fall away as they walk, a sequence of openings may release the light in stages, the distance between two objects may be the whole point, and the room may change as the body moves through it. None of that is in a frame, because a frame is simultaneous and a body is successive. Sound makes it worse, since a photograph of a work that uses sound records nothing of it, and a camera cannot hold the duration of anything, so a work whose material is time survives only as a set of instants. Scale is the other loss, and it is the one most often missed: a photograph has no size, so the height of a ceiling, the length of a floor and the distance to a wall are all flattened into a plane, and the body's relationship to them, which is the effect the space was designed to produce, disappears. What the documentation can give is therefore exact but partial: the list of components, their positions in a plan, their dimensions, materials and dates. That record is worth having and it is not a substitute, and the honest way to present it is to state the loss rather than to let the picture imply that it is the work. The same gap explains the practical difficulty: a work of this kind cannot be lent and reinstalled intact, because what would be reinstalled is the inventory, not the conditions.

questions.explanation: A full answer identifies succession, scale, light and sound as the properties a frame cannot hold, and it distinguishes the exact record of components from the missing record of experience. A weak response says only that a photograph is a poor record, without naming which properties are lost or why the loss is structural rather than a matter of equipment.
questions.hint: Ask what a photograph has that the work does not, and what the work has that a photograph cannot have.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the market's own figures make the stronger critique
questions.learningObjective: evaluate why a critique built on the target's own evidence is stronger
questions.stem: Explain why a work that prices the market in the market's own terms is a stronger critique than one that merely condemns the market.

answer.exemplar: The reason is evidentiary, and it can be stated in one line: a critique built from the target's own records can be checked, and a critique built from assertion cannot. A work that sets out, in the format of banknotes, the prices at which named artists recently sold gives its audience figures that come from the trade rather than from the artist's rhetoric. That has three consequences. The accusation is specific, so it can be answered with a figure instead of a feeling. It is falsifiable, so the artist has a stake in being right, which is what distinguishes a critique from a performance of one. And it reaches the audience the market serves, since the people who buy the work are the people who set the prices being printed, so the target cannot treat the accusation as coming from outside. There is also a deeper effect. The work's force depends on the system it attacks, since the prices mean what they mean because the market assigned them, so the piece is inside the thing it criticises, and that discomfort is part of the argument. A pure denunciation fails on every count: it restates a position the reader may already hold, produces nothing that can be verified, and can be turned round at no cost, since anyone may answer that the market is the only thing that pays artists. What the priced critique cannot do is flatter itself: the risk is that the numbers become the content and the argument disappears into an inventory, and the best work of this kind keeps a tension between the figures and what is being asked of the viewer. A weak answer praises the tactic without saying what evidence does, or condemns the market without showing what the chosen work adds to the condemnation.

questions.explanation: A full answer says why verifiable figures in the target's own terms are stronger than assertion, and it also notes the dependency that makes such a work uncomfortable, and the risk that the figures swamp the argument. A weak response only praises the strategy or only condemns the market.
questions.hint: Ask who supplied the numbers, and what a reader could do with them that a complaint would not allow.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Exposure time and the amount of light
questions.learningObjective: compute the ratio of light between two exposure times
questions.stem: At a fixed aperture the light reaching the film is proportional to the length of the exposure, so the two change together. An exposure of one sixtieth of a second is shortened to one two-hundred-and-fortieth of a second. How many times less light reaches the film?
questions.explanation: The two times are compared by dividing the longer by the shorter: one sixtieth divided by one two-hundred-and-fortieth is the same as two hundred and forty divided by sixty, which is four. So the film is open for one quarter of the time and receives one quarter of the light, and to keep the same density of image the aperture would have to be opened by two stops or the film made correspondingly more sensitive. The relation holds because exposure is a product of time and aperture, and it is the reason a short exposure can freeze a moving subject while a long one records it as a blur. A film that was open for one eightieth of a second would receive three times this amount of light.
questions.hint: Put the two times over a common denominator and divide one by the other.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: How many images a video contains
questions.learningObjective: compute the number of frames in a projected video of a given length
questions.stem: A video work is projected in its entirety for ten minutes at twenty-four separate images each second, and every image is counted as one frame of the work. How many frames does the projection present?
questions.explanation: The minutes have to become seconds before they can be multiplied by the rate: ten minutes is six hundred seconds, and six hundred seconds at twenty-four frames a second is fourteen thousand four hundred. The point of the calculation is the unit. A video is not a single image that lasts a long time, it is a very large number of discrete images shown in succession, and that is what gives the form its capacity for argument through order, pace and juxtaposition, and what makes it fragile: the work only exists as the play-back, and every frame is a unit that a cutting room can rearrange. The rate is also not fixed by the art, since other works are projected at other numbers of frames per second and at other sizes.
questions.hint: Convert the running time to seconds, then multiply by the number of frames in each second.
